## Rosenbrock time steps with adaptive step size (`rosenbrock2_step`, `adaptive_advance`) {#sec-ch09-rosenbrock}

### Summary

Stiff photochemistry needs implicit time steps, and a Newton iteration on each step can stall when the step is large.
The two-stage Rosenbrock method used here is linearly implicit: it solves two linear systems with the same frozen
Jacobian and needs no iteration. It is second order and gives an embedded error estimate. A separate controller
advances a fixed time interval by trying a step, rejecting it if the result is non-finite, strongly negative or
unreasonably large, and halving and retrying.

::: {.callout-note title="At a glance"}
**Purpose.** One second-order linearly implicit step, @eq-ch09-rosenbrock-ros2; a reject-and-halve controller.

**Data.** State `(ncol, nlyr, nspecies)` in and out; step $\Delta t$ in the caller's time unit.

**Placement.** Called by the caller's time loop; the controller wraps any `step_fn(state, dt)`.

**Activation.** API: `rosenbrock2_step`, `adaptive_advance`, `stage_schedule`.

**Guarantee / limits.** Second order, observed 1.93 at 64 steps (run `[R3]`); the controller ignores the error estimate.

**Evidence.** See the Tests layer.
:::

Local symbols: $\gamma = 1 + 1/\sqrt2$; $f(c) = \mathsf T c + S(c)$; $\mathsf A$, the stage matrix; $k_1$, $k_2$, the
stage increments; $y_2$, the intermediate state. $\mathsf L$ and $\Delta t$ are those of @sec-ch09-assembly.

### Derivation

The scheme is the two-stage Rosenbrock method of Verwer, Spee, Blom and Hundsdorfer (1999,
[doi:10.1137/S1064827597326651](https://doi.org/10.1137/S1064827597326651)) in the form the code uses:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathsf A &= \frac{\mathsf I}{\gamma \Delta t} - \mathsf L , \\
k_1 &= \mathsf A^{-1} f(c^{0}) , \\
y_2 &= c^{0} + k_1 / \gamma , \\
k_2 &= \mathsf A^{-1}\left[f(y_2) - \frac{2}{\gamma \Delta t} k_1\right] , \\
c^{1} &= c^{0} + \frac{3}{2\gamma} k_1 + \frac{1}{2\gamma} k_2 ,
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch09-rosenbrock-ros2}

with the embedded error $\lvert c^{1} - y_2 \rvert$. @eq-ch09-rosenbrock-ros2 is computed in `rosenbrock2_step`
({{< code python/atm2d/rosenbrock.py rosenbrock2_step >}}); both solves use one matrix, so its factorization is
computed once. The method is second order for any Jacobian $\mathsf L$, exact or not (the cited paper); run `[R3]`
measures the order on a linear decay.

The controller `adaptive_advance` ({{< code python/atm2d/timestep.py adaptive_advance >}}) advances a total
$\Delta t_{\mathrm{target}}$: it tries $\min(\Delta t_{\mathrm{next}}, \mathrm{remaining})$, accepts the result if
`default_accept` passes it, grows the next attempt by `grow_factor` (2) after an acceptance and multiplies by
`shrink_factor` (0.5) after a rejection. `stage_schedule` produces geometric target steps
$\min(\Delta t_0\, g^{k}, \Delta t_{\max})$.

### Numerical method

A Rosenbrock step builds the transport matrix, linearizes the sources at $c^{0}$, solves for $k_1$, re-evaluates
$f$ at $y_2$ (the Jacobian is not rebuilt), solves for $k_2$, and returns $c^{1}$ clipped at zero by default. The entry
state is restored on every exit. A non-finite stage returns the entry state with `finite=False`. The relative error is
$\max \lvert c^{1} - y_2\rvert / \lvert c^{1}\rvert$, computed after the clip, optionally only over cells whose entry
and end values exceed `error_floor`, and with the bottom layer excluded when a post-process hook is given.

`default_accept` rejects a candidate that is non-finite, has a value below $-10^{-3}$ times the species' largest
absolute entry (floored at 1), or exceeds $10^{30}$. After a rejection at $\Delta t_r$, every later attempt within the
same call is held below $\Delta t_r$ (`min_rejected`).

Setup checks and errors a user can hit: a non-positive `dt_target`; "dt collapsed below floor" after
`max_subdivisions` (16) halvings; a non-positive schedule length.

No test in `tests/` calls `rosenbrock2_step`: its order and error estimate have no kintera test at the pin (missing
evidence beyond run `[R3]`).

Runs[^ch09-r23] (pinned `python/atm2d` source, torch 2.10.0, CPU, float64). `[R3]`: $\mathrm d c/\mathrm d t = -c$ on
one cell from $c = 1$ to $t = 1$ with 8, 16, 32 and 64 steps gives errors $5.624 \times 10^{-3}$,
$1.648 \times 10^{-3}$, $4.496 \times 10^{-4}$ and $1.177 \times 10^{-4}$, observed orders 1.771, 1.874 and 1.934,
approaching 2. `[R2]`: advancing 8 time units from a first attempt of 1, with only that first attempt rejected,
accepts 16 steps all of size 0.5; the step never grows back to 1.

### Limits

`adaptive_advance` does not use the Rosenbrock error estimate: acceptance is only finiteness, a negativity threshold
and a magnitude cap, so a step can be accepted with a large truncation error. The ceiling after a rejection is
deliberate and tested, but it lasts for the whole call, so one early rejection fixes the step for the rest of the
interval (run `[R2]`). The error estimate is formed after clipping at zero. A cell clipped to zero has
$\lvert c^{1} - y_2 \rvert = \lvert y_2 \rvert$ divided by the smallest positive floating-point number, so with the
default `error_floor` of 0 one clipped cell with $y_2 \ne 0$ sets an enormous relative error (verified by reading the
formula; not run). A caller using the estimate for step control should set `error_floor`.

[^ch09-r23]: `src/kintera_report/ch09/runs/atm2d_run.py`, output `atm2d_run.out`, lines `[R2]` and `[R3]`.
